paper_title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language models increasingly serve as core decision engines within complex systems for tasks such as routing requests (Ong et al., 2024), evaluating responses (Zheng et al., 2023), and deciding the next steps of agents (Yao et al., 2023). Generating text to make categorical choices wastes computational resources on unnecessary tokens and increases latency, leading to the emergence of Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) and other specialized decision models (StartLux, 2026; Open-Jev, 2026) for these tasks. These models typically process extensive context, such as lengthy conversation or an agent trajectory, to answer several questions about it, outputting probability distributions over multiple discrete choices. When deployed on every routed request and agent action, with strict thresholds acting on their probabilities (Decision Index, 2026), these confidence-sensitive models call for an inference engine that is both fast and precise. However, current inference engines severely constrain the application of decision models since they are optimized for text generation, where the fundamental unit of work is single linear sequence. When processing decisions, frameworks like vLLM (vLLM Project, 2026d) and SGLang (SGLang Project, 2026c) treat every 1 2 Li et al. question as an independent prompt, rendering, tokenizing and scheduling the shared context once for every question. The latest vLLM computes the shared context of request once before its questions (vLLM Project, 2026b), yet every question still runs as sequence of its own and resumes from the prefix cache. On hybrid architectures this cache restores recurrent states only at block boundaries (Pan et al., 2025; Jing et al., 2026), and every question and every agent step thus computes the tokens past the last boundary again. Alternatively, multi-item scoring (SGLang Project, 2026a) appends all questions to single context with delimiter token before each. Every question then reads this extra token, which changes its hidden states and corrupts its output probabilities compared to isolated prompts (SGLang Project, 2026b). Furthermore, under dynamic batching, the order of floating-point sums changes with the batch (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), which can yield fluctuating decisions for the identical request under varying server loads. All of these issues severely compromise the reliability and efficiency of decision model serving. The root cause is mismatch between the logical structure of decision request and the physical structure in which current engines execute it. Logically, the questions of request are separate branches of tree whose trunk is the shared state, and each branch must see only the trunk and itself. Physically, these branches should run together over single copy of the trunk, which speeds up inference by computing the trunk only once and letting many short branches fill the GPU in one pass. Generation engines tie the physical layout to the logical one, running every question as separate sequence that computes or reloads the trunk again. Multi-item scoring ties them the other way and does run the branches together. Yet it writes the tree into the sequence itself, and its delimiter tokens enter the input of every branch and, as Figure 1 illustrates, shift the probabilities and flip decisions. Closing this gap means running the branches together while each still computes exactly what it would compute alone, so the physical stream must keep apart the branches it places side by side. An attention layer can keep them apart with mask, yet the Gated DeltaNet layers (Yang et al., 2025) of hybrid models such as Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026) fold every earlier token into one recurrent state, through which branch would inherit its siblings. Separating the branches there requires each of them to restart from the exact state of its trunk, inside the same pass that computes the trunk. To address this, we propose Flide (Flat-Graph Inference for Decision Models), an efficient and exact inference engine that separates the logical structure of decision requests from their physical execution on the GPU. Flide lays round of requests out as one flat token stream and records their dependencies in GPU-resident metadata. With ForkAttention, the attention and Gated DeltaNet layers follow these dependencies, and in exact arithmetic every question computes what it would compute alone. Since the request structure is encoded in data, small set of recorded execution graphs can serve different request compositions. The same state-forking mechanism also supports growing agent histories, allowing later requests to resume from checkpoints saved during earlier inference passes. In addition, an optional batch-invariant mode fixes floating-point reduction orders to keep answers bitwise identical across server loads. We evaluate Flide against state-of-the-art inference engines on workloads ranging from one question per passage to articles and agent trajectories with many questions. Experimental results show that Flide answers up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang on public hybrid models and leads on dedicated decision models. Its throughput leads at every concurrency level whenever shared state carries several questions. Meanwhile, as multi-item scoring shifts probabilities to gain throughput, Flide yields outputs closest to the float32 reference distributions in total variation distance. These results establish that separating the logical structure of decision requests from their physical execution lets an inference engine be exact and fast at once. Our contributions are threefold. We trace both the repeated computation and the shifted answers of current engines to one root cause, the coupling between the logical structure of decision request and its physical execution. We propose Flide, which keeps each request as tree in GPU metadata while running every round as one flat stream, and forks every state exactly with ForkAttention. On public hybrid and decision models, Flide answers up to an order of magnitude faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to the float32 reference in total variation.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Prefix Sharing and State Branching. Modern serving systems reduce redundant computation by caching key-value representations of reusable prompt prefixes (Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024a,b). Specialized execution kernels retrieve these cached representations during decoding via cascade attention (Ye et al., 2025; Juravsky et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2024) or sequence-tree traversals (Yao et al., 2025). For hybrid architectures containing recurrent states (Gu and Dao, 2023; Yang et al., 2025), existing frameworks either constrain state materialization to coarse block boundaries (Pan et al., 2025; vLLM Project, 2026c; Jing et al., Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking 3 Engine One pass Same input Hybrid fork Graph replay Bitwise vLLM (vLLM Project, 2026d) SGLang (SGLang Project, 2026c) SGLang MIS (SGLang Project, 2026a) vllm-jev (mode-io, 2026) Flide Table 1. Each mark follows the public documentation and code of the engine, and bitwise marks an optional mode that keeps answers bit-identical under any load on hybrid models. 2026) or require predefined checkpoint positions (Shirokikh and Nikolenko, 2026). Speculative decoding verifies token trees with tree attention (Miao et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2024), and its hybrid variants propagate recurrent states along the branches (Wu et al., 2025; Ghantasala, 2026; Ma, 2026). Domain-specific frontends fork requests into isolated sequences that query shared prefix cache (Zheng et al., 2024a). However, all of these mechanisms mandate strict temporal separation where shared prefixes must complete execution and populate memory buffers before downstream queries can consume them. Flide eliminates this decoupled caching phase by evaluating both the shared context and every branching question within single forward pass, dynamically propagating both attention and Gated DeltaNet states across flattened token sequence. Decision Model Serving and Execution Exactness. Decision-making architectures operate under strict latency budgets and rely on well-calibrated categorical distributions (TypeSafe AI, 2026; OneJev Team, 2026; Open-Jev, 2026; vLLM Semantic Router, 2026). Existing engines handle these single-token workloads either by processing questions as isolated sequences (Du et al., 2025; vLLM Project, 2026d; SGLang Project, 2026c), which repeats prefix calculations, or by concatenating candidate queries with delimiter tokens (SGLang Project, 2026a), which invalidates isolated query semantics and requires CPU-managed segmentation that breaks CUDA graph capture. Standard graph capture strategies mitigate prefill dispatch overhead by padding requests to static shapes (SGLang Team, 2026), but still treat the individual sequence as the primitive unit of execution. Even when the prefix is computed once beforehand (vLLM Project, 2026b), every question resumes from the cache as sequence of its own. Other specialized variants incur latency penalties by scanning block masks (Chouhan and Perry, 2026; Antunes et al., 2026), packing spoken input streams into eager passes (Jin et al., 2026), or evaluating candidate trees across segmented passes (Ma et al., 2026). Compounding these systemic overheads, LLM serving engines let co-scheduled requests change the outputs of one another, whereas database systems share work across concurrent queries while keeping each query isolated (Sellis, 1988). Prefix cache substitutions create observable discrepancies compared to isolated evaluation (Patodiya, 2026), and dynamic reduction orders cause floating-point nondeterminism (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Existing batch-invariant kernels slow serving by 34 percent on Qwen3-8B in SGLang (SGLang Team, 2025), and the batch-invariant mode of vLLM cannot execute recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers (vLLM Project, 2026a). Flide resolves these scheduling and numerical conflicts simultaneously by executing multi-branch rounds through GPU-resident metadata. This approach preserves full CUDA graph replay across dynamic workloads while every answer equals its standalone computation in exact arithmetic. As summarized in Table 1, Flide is the only one of these engines that concurrently achieves single-pass execution, unpolluted query inputs, arbitrary hybrid state branching, CUDA graph replaying, and an optional bitwise-invariant mode under dynamic loads.

sections.title: 3.2 ForkAttention
sections.content: To resolve the first challenge, ForkAttention structures each decision request as computational tree where the shared state forms common trunk and the questions fork as independent branches. Evaluating the shared trunk once allows every question to inherit the prefix representation without redundant computation or prompt modifications. Pointwise operations, including linear projections, normalization layers, and multilayer perceptrons, remain indifferent to this tree structure because they process each token in complete isolation. State forking therefore requires intervention only in the token-mixing layers, which must grant questions access to the shared trunk while isolating sibling branches from each other. Flide maps this tree onto the GPU by flattening an entire round of requests into single continuous token stream without padding. sections.title: 3.3 Flat-Graph Execution
sections.content: Flat-graph execution resolves the second challenge by turning the forks of round into GPU work with negligible launch overhead, as illustrated in Figure 2(c). short decision request on small model takes only few milliseconds of GPU time, which launching several thousand kernels one by one would dominate. Although CUDA graphs eliminate these sequential launches, captured graph fixes the shape of every kernel launch, whereas server encounters rounds containing requests of highly variable numbers and lengths. To 6 Li et al. reconcile this, Flide keeps the tree of round purely as GPU data. The shape of every launch then depends on the length of the flat stream alone, and small collection of captured graphs accommodates any mix of requests and questions. 3.3.1 GPU-Resident Metadata All variables determined by the round composition, including segment lengths, positional indices, key ranges, and state indices, reside in compact device buffers populated before graph replay, from which every kernel derives its workload. The attention kernel fetches keys from two sources, the shared state of the request and the querys specific question, and skips the states of other requests interleaved in the stream. The kernel constructs its tile table directly on the GPU, loads the fully visible key blocks without applying mask, and restricts masking exclusively to partially visible blocks. The Gated DeltaNet layers iterate over list of fixed-length chunks populated by each round, with any unused entries beyond the active chunks returning immediately. Consequently, altering the mix of requests only modifies the buffer contents while preserving the exact launch configuration of the captured graph. 3.3.2 Graphs over Stream Lengths Building on length-bucketed CUDA graph capture (SGLang Team, 2026), Flide allows rounds with different decision-tree structures to reuse the same captured graph. At server initialization, Flide captures family of flat graphs indexed by stream capacity 𝑇. Each graph also reserves fixed capacities for requests, question segments, Gated DeltaNet chunks, and readout rows. The actual request boundaries and question dependencies are supplied through GPU-resident metadata, allowing different request mixes to share the same execution graph. For each round, Flide selects the smallest graph whose buffers can accommodate both its flattened stream and associated metadata. Tokens are packed without padding between requests; padding occurs only at the tail, where dense layers still perform computation but no valid token accesses the padded positions. If round exceeds the largest graphs capacity, Flide splits it along request boundaries into multiple replays. An individual request exceeding this capacity runs through the same flat-stream execution without CUDA graph replay. 3.3.3 Selective Readout The output head of Equation 1 reads only the last token of every question, so in the final layer every token still contributes its keys and values while the rest of the layer, its MLP included, runs only at these rows. An index buffer of fixed size in every graph holds the rows, which skips most of the final-layer work without changing any output in exact arithmetic.

sections.title: 3.4 Incremental State Forking
sections.content: Successive steps of an agent trajectory often share most of their state, and therefore most of the trunk of their decision trees. Flide exploits this overlap by checkpointing the state of request at an internal position 𝑚. later request can resume from the checkpoint when its tokens up to 𝑚 match. Each checkpoint stores the float32 recurrent state and convolution window of every Gated DeltaNet layer at 𝑚, together with the keys and values of the full-attention layers before 𝑚. This allows resumed request to compute the same function as fresh one in exact arithmetic. Flide places 𝑚 slightly before the end of state so that tokens likely to change at the next step, such as those at the end of conversational turn, fall after the checkpoint. Flide generates the checkpoint during the same forward pass that computes the requests answers. To achieve this, Flide divides the state segments of the stream into two levels at their checkpoints. Each Gated DeltaNet layer processes the two levels sequentially, saving the final states of the first level as checkpoints and passing them to the second through the same state-indexing mechanism used for question forking. For full attention, cached keys and values precede newly computed ones in buffer representing each states history, allowing resumed states to be processed without occupying contiguous span of the flat stream. At each agent step, Flide thus computes the new tokens and short uncached tail only once for all questions, saves checkpoint for the next step, and forks the questions from the completed state, as illustrated in Figure 2(d).

sections.title: 4.1 Settings
sections.content: Workloads. We build six workloads from four public datasets, RACE (Lai et al., 2017), QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022), MultiRC (Khashabi et al., 2018) and the Decision Index (Decision Index, 2026). Two of them send one question per state, with RACE passages and with QuALITY articles cut to 3,600 tokens. The other four send every question of state in one request, as the datasets come, from four questions per RACE passage to 48 per MultiRC paragraph on average, as Table 2 lists and Appendix details. Baselines. We compare against vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024a) through their decision endpoints, against SGLangs multi-item scoring (SGLang Project, 2026a), MIS in the tables, and on the dedicated decision models against vllm-jev (mode-io, 2026) and its RadixFlow scheduler (Jing et al., 2026). vLLM, SGLang and Flide serve the instruct models of Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026) from 0.8B to 27B and of Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026) from E2B to 31B, multi-item scoring the Qwen3.5 models and vllm-jev Open-Jev-2B and Open-Jev-9B (Open-Jev, 2026), all in bfloat16 with CUDA graphs on, except multi-item scoring, which turns them off. Flide and vLLM read the same prompts, while SGLang and vllm-jev render their own templates, and Appendix lists the versions and settings of every engine. Metrics. Lat. is the median latency in milliseconds of request from single client, and C8, C32 and C64 are the requests per second under 8, 32 and 64 closed-loop clients. Against float32 forward pass of the same model, Agr. is the share of questions with the same top answer, TV the mean total variation distance in points, P99 the 99th percentile of the largest change in one options probability, and Flip the share of decisions that threshold of 0.5 takes differently. Acc. is the share of correct answers, and Stab. the share of questions whose top answer at 64 clients equals the one at single client. Setup. All measurements run on one NVIDIA H200 GPU, with the engines started one after another and every prefix cache emptied before each level. Every row is sent four times, twice for DI and the full QuALITY articles, and each copys state starts with its own tag, which keeps any request from reusing the state of another.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we presented Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine for decision models that decouples the logical tree structure of each request from its physical execution within single flattened token stream. By leveraging ForkAttention, Flide forks intermediate states precisely across both attention and recurrent layers, replaying arbitrary execution rounds through compact pre-recorded graphs while extending agent histories directly from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. This architecture resolves the fundamental conflict between hierarchical request logic and sequential token execution, eliminating both the redundant prefix computations and the delimiter tokens that shift the answers of existing serving engines. Extensive evaluations across hybrid and full-attention architectures, specialized decision benchmarks, and real-world agent trajectories demonstrate that Flide achieves substantial speedups over current state-of-the-art frameworks while staying closest to the float32 reference distributions on Qwen3.5. By unifying high-throughput parallel execution with strict mathematical exactness, Flide establishes principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in next-generation LLM agent systems.

sections.content: Table 18 lists the decision models that Flide serves, each against its release engine on the first 32 requests of RACE, MultiRC and QuALITY, of 760-request sample of the Decision Index and of GQA with images. Both mammoth and elephant read each block both ways in their full-attention layers, and since their state never reads question, their questions still fork it under the rule of Section 3.2 without 𝑡𝑦 𝑡𝑥. Jeffan, StartLux and Lychee read the whole prompt of each question both ways, so every question runs as sequence of its own in the stream, and pplx-decider reads all questions of request in one sequence. Intern-Decision reads at most 16 questions request, so its cells keep the requests within that limit among the first 32. The Open-Jev row repeats RACE and QuALITY of Table 6, all 256 requests against the better setting of vllm-jev, and adds DI and MultiRC on their first 32 requests against the same setting. The OneJev row compares OneJev1.5-0.8B with qev, the engine it ran on before Flide, on all 760 requests of the DI sample and the first 32 of MultiRC and QuALITY. Models built on Qwen3.8, which shares the architecture of Qwen3.5, appear in the table with Qwen3.5 backbone.
